text: Some people come to Wassu looking for answers.
They want to know who built the circles, exactly when, exactly why.
They want the story — beginning, middle, end — neatly told.
The stones do not offer that.
What the stones offer instead is something more disorienting and more useful: the sheer fact of human effort across time.
Someone decided, 2,000 years ago, that the dead were worth marking.
That the labour of cutting stone and moving it and raising it in a circle was a worthy expression of something — grief, love, status, belief, community — that demanded to be made permanent.
And then someone else decided the same thing.
The people of The Gambia who live near Wassu today are not the same communities who built the circles.
Languages have changed, kingdoms have come and gone.

But the stones are still here, and the people are still here, and between them — between the very old stones and the very living people — there is a conversation about what it means to belong to a place, to come from something, to leave something behind.
Stand inside one of the circles.
Let the stones ask you their question.
You don't need to have an answer.
You just need to hear it.
